posts.cooked:
Thusfar, the only real concerns that I have surround the Scene Tracker and its relationship with Initiative.  It just feels like too much of a meta-game to me, with the game actively punishing players for wanting to go before the villains.  In fact, doing so outright penalizes players for taking a "surprise round" against villains.

To me, that's an easy fix:

1) The environment/scene tracker always goes last in initiative order.  

2) The environment does not get to 'choose' who goes next; the last player (or GM) to take a turn chooses who starts the next round (following the Environment/Scene Tracker).

3) The GM may not pass initiative to themselves, even if they have multiple actors within the scene, unless all players have already gone.

4) Any player who chooses to pass initiative to the GM may, on their next turn, reroll a single die of their choice.

Yes, this doesn't "eliminate" the possibility of the players all going before the villain, but it does disincentivize doing so, as a player can reap a tangible, in-game benefit by passing play to the GM.  Further, it makes GM tracking easier, by keeping the scene tracker's place in initiative static.

posts.cooked:
My opinions haven't really changed, although they've become more refined in some ways.

  • Most of my concerns were about the adventure modules in the starter kit, not the core rules.  Obviously, nothing has changed my mind about those.
  • Challenges that are set up as one or more Overcome checks that need to be made really need to be spelled out, or else players won't bite on them.  Ones that are required need to be hand-fed to the players (e.g. written on index cards right off the bat).  Optional ones can be hinted at or "gated" behind other events or attempts, but the GM needs to assume that they won't go anywhere, and balance challenges appropriately.
  • Challenges are still pretty railroad-y.  The GM decides what needs to be done, the players figure out some way to justify their Powers and Qualities (and ideally a Principle) to accomplish it.  Sometimes that can result in some cool storytelling, but other times it was really strained.
  • If you want to design an effective character, the single most important thing is to choose two Principles that let you use your Max die in the widest possible range of circumstances.  Ones that require specific circumstances (Cosmic), that are hard to justify (Time Traveler, at least when you're from the past), or that don't let you use your Max die (Speed) make it so that you'll rack up a lot more failures and twists, and miss opportunities for Hero Points.  Choosing your other abilities wisely helps (especially mass attacks and persistent boosts/hinders), but the Principles are critical.
  • Christopher made a big point out of playing by the rules (except for the mecha battle and the cheer boosts), but he did exploit the vagueness of the rules extensively.  The twists he came up with were frequently much more or much less powerful than the recommended ones in the book.  A GM that's just a little off in their judgment could make adventures much harder or much easier than intended.
  • Regarding initiative: the players got fatigued.  Early on, they tried to choose their turn order very carefully to avoid negative consequences.  Later, they started making their choices almost at random.  They completely gave up on using abilities that lasted until their next turn, and never bothered setting up combos with boosts and hinders.  Christopher stopped exploiting every mistake they made, too, probably because he didn't want to punish them for it anymore (like he did in the first couple of games).  So I don't feel like the system ended up working well.
  • The system is really straightforward, but it's still fiddly for inexperienced players.  Maggie and Rae forgot about their inherent abilities and reactions nearly every time they would have been relevant.  Rae took basically the whole game to understand the difference between abilities and powers/qualities.  They all invoked their hero points and collected trades only rarely.  Having taught D&D to new players, especially 4th edition, I feel like there's a gap here--D&D is overall a much more complicated game, but it's less error-prone to get started with.
  • The Scene Tracker is indeed iffy sometimes.  The villain being able to accelerate it is particularly problematic--when that happens, the players run a real risk of losing due to it.  A villain that really "wants to win" will be better off accelerating the scene tracker than trying to damage the heroes.  Of course, the system is designed such that the GM really can't go all-out trying to "beat" the players, otherwise they'll just have a bunch of minions gang up on one hero.
  • The game isn't about "progression."  It just isn't, get over it.  On the plus side, that means it's well-suited for shorter series and one-shots.  I think people who want to play campaigns of 20+ sessions will start feeling bored with their characters, but then, the superhero genre really isn't about that.  I think Critical Hits could design a spinoff system in a fantasy/sci-fi setting that used the core Sentinels system and build a new game with leveled progression, but that would be something else entirely.

Thoughts and notes after watching the character creation session and Issue #1.  I will follow up with more as I go.

Character creation uses random die rolls.  I am kind of curious what the purpose of this is.  It seemed a little bit tacked on, maybe to satisfy people who just want random dice rolls because reasons.  Maybe useful for generating ideas if you really just don't know.  Maybe someone on the design team has some deeper insights here though.  I know games I like have seemingly weird stuff in character creation that actually works nicely in practice (Name lists in dungeon world, for example).  

Character creation might be a little bit lenghty.  It might be something that can be done individually outside of an actual play session though, at least in part, which can mitigate this.  This is not a concern, just an observation.

 

A lot of what you get when listening to a charismatic storyteller like Christopher is going to have nothing to do with the game itself, and everything to do with the person running the game.  So it requires some careful attention to separate out the two parts of this, and without the rules in front of me to reference, I still can't fully differentiate between what is the GM and what is the rules.  So everything has to be taken with a grain of salt.

At 26 minutes in to the first issue, Christopher asks Craig to make an overcome roll to investigate an energy signature he detects.  Its not entirely clear what the point of having him role here is.  Is there a specific rule that says when a roll is triggered, or is it just GM discretion?  Is the GM just using this as a generic "investigate roll", with all the problems that come with that?  What would have happened if he had failed the investigation roll?  My guess is that things would have worked out almost identically, because saying "You find nothing, I guess we stop playing" doesn't work for good story telling.  As it stands, his "success" did not seem very valuable.  All he got was "Thats sure some energy signature there.  Lots of magic".  Which isn't useful for him beyond saying "Go talk to your teammate" which is a given regardless of the investigation result.  Even if he hadn't been given the detail that it was magical, one of the other 3 player would have been given that detail, since they had even more ability to understand magic than he did.  

Another overcome role is made at the 54 minute mark.  This one the GM rules that one of the players principles can't be used, but when the player fails, the "major twist" is just that the previously overruled principle kicks in and gives the information anyways.  Again, what are the actual rules on overcomes and investigations?  Do the rules explicitly tell GMs not to do these time wasting behaviors, and the GM here just didn't care, or do they not give any meaningful guidance at all?  Do the rules actually encourage this self defeating behavior?  This one isn't quite as bad as the first one I mentioned.  Its actually possible for the adventure to continue here without successful knowledge checks.

This next one is less of a complaint about the game, and more a complaint about the way designers and fans have inaccurately described the game.  There are multiple points where mechanical decisions are made before the fiction is consulted, sometimes without even bothering to check the fiction.  Two examples:  Starblight gets chomped by a dragon and the GM informs the player that his next turn can only be an overcome action.  Later, Violet Heart uses a rage ribbons attack against some minions.  The attack misses, meaning the minions are not destroyed but they are reduced a die size.  No one ever says what this means in the fiction though.  This is probably fine.  It might be tedious, in this particular system, to always go back to the fiction.  But the fact that this is even possible shows that the game is fundamentally incompatible with PbtA design principles.  So its frustrating that so many people, including the actual designers of the game, have claimed Apocalypse World is a source for the design, when it absolutely is not, at least in the presented materials we have.

To answer lynfox question. This system speaks to me on a very base level. I get it and love it. There was no new surprise, just happy to see things working. I was really please on Christopher making the encounter using the rules they made.

To answer a few complaints:

-I ran this game over the Course of the last year (and a half) and the Scene tracker is not bad, it adds tension and gets people focused. only once I have gone over it (only minions where left) and summed up that fight quickly. As a player, I constantly advance the tracker early on to get to that sweet yellow zone. If you are worried about the scene tracker going to fast, don't have the villains or environments use abilities to advance the tracker.  Christopher even said to make it longer. But please try it out before making any changes to it.

-At Gen Con Dave ran me though Character generation, it was fairly painless. I take as the dice rolls as a way to help guide your character, you might find some interesting path to take your hero(I had an idea in mind and it all worked out). Getting to retcon and adjust a few things really smooths out the process. NightMist secret Apprentice, Olrac(still workshopping name) is now ready for prime time!

-When a minion die gets reduced it means it was damaged but not taken out of the battle. Christopher does a good job at describing this other time he shows this game off not sure if he said it here or not.

- When I first start a game to teach people, I start players by rolling an overcome to noticed the inciting incident. This is done to help teach player how to roll dice, and about twist. Very rarely does someone not take a twist (even a major one). And if they do fail I just find another way to add them to the story. 

-In Startblight's overcome to get out of the dragon scene. He states that damage will not get him out, nor defend, boost/hinder. He has to come up with a description on how to get out, and roll dice to make it happen. I believe Adam talk about what he will do.

I assumed it would be that Dynamo finds something else that distracts him, or misinterprets the data. Enough to send them in the right direction, but not enough to fully prepare them. I've also been assuming that rolls are triggered when there is a chance for failure as in every other game. As for a generic roll, yeah, Overcome is pretty much the everything roll, with obvious exceptions for the other moves.

 

Jay Green:

Another overcome role is made at the 54 minute mark.  This one the GM rules that one of the players principles can't be used, but when the player fails, the "major twist" is just that the previously overruled principle kicks in and gives the information anyways.

I think, although I might be misremembering, that the major twist was a compulsion to act in a certain way on the next turn. All the principle would have let Starblight do is use his max die, not being able to use it doesn't prevent him from using any powers or qualities. He can still use the Blightmatrix to learn stuff related to laser dragons (sorry, lazer, I guess) which is how he still succeeds but it is at a cost.

 

As for the PbtA points, in the fiction you always manage to hit an opponent. Being reduced in size is a wound, rather than a knockout. Christopher is better at narrating this in later episodes. and the whole "Must use an Overcome" thing is, I think, because the pressing matter was that Starblight was being eaten and probably shouldn't stick around in the mouth.
 I can totally see the PbtA influence. The system is built around soft hits driving the narrative. Sure, there're other influences (I think FATE is one of them) and obviously the villains get a turn unlike in PbtA, but everything is designed around moving the fiction forwards. Christopher makes a big point in the other issues about asking the players HOW they do things, not WHAT they are doing, to reinforce the fiction. Even the superhero powers (the GYRO things, not the dice) alter the basic moves like some PbtA playbook moves.

I hope this has made sense and/or helped in any way.

posts.cooked:
@MindWanderer

 

I feel like that most of your concerns about the system are concerns that are about any new system - If a GM is not experienced in the system, there is lots of room for error. I am not sure that I can muster up much worry/concern over a lot of them - 

MindWanderer:

My opinions haven't really changed, although they've become more refined in some ways.

  • Most of my concerns were about the adventure modules in the starter kit, not the core rules.  Obviously, nothing has changed my mind about those.

*Challenges that are set up as one or more Overcome checks that need to be made really need to be spelled out, or else players won't bite on them.  Ones that are required need to be hand-fed to the players (e.g. written on index cards right off the bat).  Optional ones can be hinted at or "gated" behind other events or attempts, but the GM needs to assume that they won't go anywhere, and balance challenges appropriately.

*Challenges are still pretty railroad-y.  The GM decides what needs to be done, the players figure out some way to justify their Powers and Qualities (and ideally a Principle) to accomplish it.  Sometimes that can result in some cool storytelling, but other times it was really strained.

 

All of these concerns, while completely valid, are about how experienced a GM/Player/group is. The more experienced the group with freeform RPG style (FATE comes to mind, and there are a couple of other systems I can't recall the name of off the top of my head but are far less constrained rules wise, than say DnD) the less these concerns become a issue, in my view. I feel like that is an inherent thing about -any- 'less than mechanically rigid' system, and if you really want to get the most out of Roleplaying its a concern about -every- system. 

You can have skill checks in DnD,WoD,FATE, which the players need to figure out there is something to do, just like these Overcome Checks. - Certainly in a game of DnD you could not haver any skill checks and just have combat, but then its not a RPG its a tactical battle game. If players walk into a bar and need to find the hidden entrance into the sewers, thats a skill check. Its also an Overcome check in this sytem. If players are in a battle and their spells aren't working to hit the wizard, but the scene description said he had a big crystal on a pedastal behind him - thats a skill check to figure out how to get past his shield. Or an Overcome in this system.

Your concerns that the players may not know to do this or bite on it are valid - but they are valid for every game. If players are not going to think to act outside of 'Me Kronk, Me Hit' then any system is going to have to GM'd differently. 

 

MindWanderer:

*If you want to design an effective character, the single most important thing is to choose two Principles that let you use your Max die in the widest possible range of circumstances.  Ones that require specific circumstances (Cosmic), that are hard to justify (Time Traveler, at least when you're from the past), or that don't let you use your Max die (Speed) make it so that you'll rack up a lot more failures and twists, and miss opportunities for Hero Points.  Choosing your other abilities wisely helps (especially mass attacks and persistent boosts/hinders), but the Principles are critical.

 

I can completely agree and yet disagree with these. If you are looking to make the most effective character that can handle the situation given in the quickest and most effective way possible, yes. You are completely right. WIthout maximizing the use of your and your groups Principles youare missing out on a lot of bonuses and more effective rolls than a standard Risky Action or Overcome check.

This I disagree with out of principle (heh) as the type of RPGer I am. I am -not- looking to be most effective in an RPG. I'm looking to tell a story, and a lot of a good story will be NOT being effective. This is clearly the type of RPGers that Christopher and Adam are - you can see it in the gleam with the Twists in Christophers eyes and why Adam almost -always- takes a twist if there is an option. Because its far more fun

In this sense, I feel a lot of the abilities are super powerful (Completely destroy X minions? wow. That can clear a scene - or some of the Boost Hinder combos? Yeah jeeze those are cool) and that relates to the 'We're SUPER HEROES' - but the Twist system is completely a storytelling mechanic to make the game interesting.

Also, I get the feeling from the way the sheets are designed that Principles are supposed to be the most important thing to your character. They are your 'Class' or your 'Clan and Bloodline' - they are what defines your character.

 

 

MindWanderer:

*Christopher made a big point out of playing by the rules (except for the mecha battle and the cheer boosts), but he did exploit the vagueness of the rules extensively. 

  • The twists he came up with were frequently much more or much less powerful than the recommended ones in the book.  A GM that's just a little off in their judgment could make adventures much harder or much easier than intended.

 

 

These are back to my first point - Experienced groups/players are going to always be better at RPGs in any system than inexperienced. This system i feel is far more friendly to inexperienced because of the lack of rules, but thats a personal opinion. I can see where you're coming from here.

 

I am curious though on how you feel he exploited the vaugness of the rules? In a bad way? (Was it confusing to the players? DId it make the game less fun?) or in a good way (to make some things roll smother, to make some things change direction if needed?)

MindWanderer:

*Regarding initiative: the players got fatigued.  Early on, they tried to choose their turn order very carefully to avoid negative consequences.  Later, they started making their choices almost at random.  They completely gave up on using abilities that lasted until their next turn, and never bothered setting up combos with boosts and hinders.  Christopher stopped exploiting every mistake they made, too, probably because he didn't want to punish them for it anymore (like he did in the first couple of games).  So I don't feel like the system ended up working well.

 

I'm interested in these points - I agree, that after a while they stopped worrying/carring about some things. I see it as some slightly different reasons. They realized that in most situations, worrying about the Badguys all going twice in a row isn't actually that big a deal - Sure they get to actions, but as a result the Heroes will get two turns in a row too. It balances out and really isn't that big a deal, so they only thought about it in extereme situations (The final boss fight)

 

As for exploiting ever mistake - thats not something I believe any GM should do.  They should exploit mistakes that make the game interesting, but if players are just being human and not their acutal SuperHuman characters, then they shouldn't be punished for that. I am not a Super Detective with a logical brain and an understanding of  connections like Sherlock Holmes/Batman/Wraith but my character might be and I shouldn't be punished because I am not smart enough to actually be that. We aren't playing ourselves, were playing Characters we want to experience, and good GM's don't exploit that difference, they help craft a story that shows that thing we want to be in the limelight.

 

MindWanderer:
  • The system is really straightforward, but it's still fiddly for inexperienced players.  Maggie and Rae forgot about their inherent abilities and reactions nearly every time they would have been relevant.  Rae took basically the whole game to understand the difference between abilities and powers/qualities.  They all invoked their hero points and collected trades only rarely.  Having taught D&D to new players, especially 4th edition, I feel like there's a gap here–D&D is overall a much more complicated game, but it's less error-prone to get started with.

 

This is another Agree/Disagree point for me - I agree, it seems like Rae had some difficulty, and never really used her abilities on her sheet - I think that isn't so much a problem with the system, as the situation. A brand new, never before played an RPG before with 2 very experienced RPGers (and one somewhat, I think Maggie has played RPGs before) is now doing so on camera before a crowd. Thats some pressure! Its hard enough for me to Roleplay out what an NPC or my Character does in front of my closest friends, trying to remember to be my character, which if you arent a naturally extroverted type can be very hard to do, and to learn a brand new system, and do that all under the watchful eyes/ears of hundreds of people?  While there are two other people in the room who have done this sort of thing for decades and are all over the system as well? Wow. I would forget a lot of stuff too.

So I don't know how good of a meter stick this is for teaching the system. 

MindWanderer:

*The Scene Tracker is indeed iffy sometimes.  The villain being able to accelerate it is particularly problematic–when that happens, the players run a real risk of losing due to it.  A villain that really "wants to win" will be better off accelerating the scene tracker than trying to damage the heroes.  Of course, the system is designed such that the GM really can't go all-out trying to "beat" the players, otherwise they'll just have a bunch of minions gang up on one hero.

*The game isn't about "progression."  It just isn't, get over it.  On the plus side, that means it's well-suited for shorter series and one-shots.  I think people who want to play campaigns of 20+ sessions will start feeling bored with their characters, but then, the superhero genre really isn't about that.  I think Critical Hits could design a spinoff system in a fantasy/sci-fi setting that used the core Sentinels system and build a new game with leveled progression, but that would be something else entirely.

 

Completely valid concerns. Completely. And you also made your own responses that I would make - thats just this system. Its not for everything, and thats fine. It does what its good at and thats what its going to do. 

Also, as a Villain is controlled by the GM, its my opinion the GM is there to facilitate the story, not to 'Win'. Win for the GM is making the players feel something, making them feel like having tears for the loss of an NPC, or rage at an villain, or fear at a situation, or horror at a concept. Not  "Beat them all into the ground" - so a villain won't necessarily do whats 'best' for his/her concept, they will do whats best to make a compelling story.

 

 

 

All of your concerns I can see the validity of, MindWanderer. They make sense. They also, in my opinion, stem from a completely different view of RPGs th an mine - you strike me as someone who far more enjoys the combat of DnD than the roleplaying - though you probably enjoy the RP as well, but when the swords come out and the magic starts getting flung about you might be someone who starts to have more fun there.

Nothing wrong with that, nothing at all. I myself am the more fluid type of player who would be just as keen to never get in a fight. Note, I am also an unashamed minmaxing Twink. I can, and have, made characters in every system I play in that can one shot baddies and completely destroy, mechanically, anything they come across - there is merit to this, which I think is why I see a lot of merit in a lot of your concerns. (This Twinkyness comes because some of my original rp group was very twinky, and in order to feel like i wasn't useless, i had to learn to be the same) My natural inclination, and when I have the most fun in table top situations with friends, is not to be that Twink, however. Its to have lots of weaknesses, and take twists and flaws and play them up to the max. Get into situations where the GM can really put the screws on us RP wise, if not mechanically, and put us in situations where we face these twists.

 

As a GM, i am -very- much a social/rp/twist GM. I love to run plots where combat is almost non existant. Where the issues are all cerebral in nature. In that feeling, this sytem is amazing. It will make what combat there is go pretty fast, and still create lots of amazing roleplaying situations - I point to Rae's moves against the big bad in the final episode - those were amazing oppertunities to tell a story! Even if she didn't use anything on her sheet other than Lunar Orb, she told a hell of an awesome story with it!

 

 

So, in conclusion, I hear your concerns (not that I can do anything about them, but I am listening!) And i feel like I understand them, even if on a basic fundamnetal level my view goes a completely opposite direction. Thank you for voicing them!

Some of my views of this system:

 

The Scene Tracker: I like the concept as it allows more rapid access to certain abilities without requiring you to take damage and builds tension. I feel the trick to the tracker is more in how it is approached. I feel people view it as a lose scenario while I treat it more as a linker between scenes that dictates the start of how the next scene starts. There is potential with it, but it will require a lot of balancing of length of tracker and repurcussions of failure as well as when to use it. The one problem I do see with it is that it actively fights boosting and defending as many characters feel that they are on a clock and are playing all out from the beginning in fear that slower strategies will not pay off. I have found the best options is to not introduce the tracker until after the scene has been going for a few rounds and the villains/environment take specific actions to initiate the need for the tracker and impending doom.

 

Initiative: This is a huge concern for me as it actively fights certain play styles, buffs, and overcomes. As noted, there is no benefit to not try and have heroes all go and then villains, the problem is that this can give villains a big advantage in how things play out. So here's my opinion on RPG's in general: The rules matter.

If you want a game that's basically freeform storytelling, you can use FATE, you can use Amber, you can use No Thank You, Evil.  Or you could use D&D, or GURPS, or anything else you want.  It doesn't make any difference.  You don't need rules that stand up to any scrutiny whatsoever.  You don't even really need a game system at all.  You're just talking and telling stories, and the GM handles things however they feel like.

What would make you choose one game system over another is how they handle mechanically.  And then you get into what rules are balanced, consistent, and smooth.  When one character is more effective than another (when it comes to mechanical/dice-based challenges), that's a strike against the system.  When a player can approach similar problems in similar ways and make similar rolls, yet get drastically different results, that's a strike.  When the rules are hard to remember, hard to execute, or require frequent lookups on a table or flipping through a book, that's a strike.

A good GM can work around even the worst rules to create a fun game.  Sometimes that involves making house rules, sometimes it's filling in ambiguities, sometimes it's avoiding parts of the system that are the most janky.  Christopher did that himself; Sir Arton had an ability that was unfun, so he stopped using it.  That's an example of having a positive experience in spite of the system rather than because of it.  Same thing with initiative: early on, Christopher was expecting a crunchier gameplay style, so when the players screwed up the initiative order, he punished them by advancing the scene tracker 4 spots at at once.  The more sessions that passed, the more he realized that they were never going to be careful tacticians, and the less he punished them for bad decisions.

The reason I bring up Overcome checks as a concern is because of how they're integrated into combat scenes.  In most other games I've played, noncombat abilities can be used or not used in a much more freeform way.  Need to find a piece of information?  You could roll dice to get the word on the street or hit up a library, but you could also role-play talking to people, or pay someone off, or use magic.  When you're in a timed scene and you see a checkbox with "rescue the civilians" next to it, you look at your Principles, Powers, and Qualities, and think up a way to justify applying them to a single roll.  It's not a bad approach, but to me it makes every challenge feel the same.  You also have the "when all you have is a hammer, every problem looks like a nail" thing going on.

I've finished as much of the stream as I am going to get to, so might as well respond to the initial misgivings I had.  The stream at least gave me confidence that the game is not doing what the starter kit advertised, which is railroady metaplot.  It was nice to see an original adventure with original characters.  

Other than that, the rules seem pretty mediocre, and the game as a whole does not know what it wants to be.  It has a lot of cool ideas smashed together, but not in a coherent or thought out way.  The playstyle seems to heavily rely on GM sensibilities as to what should happen next, with the rules just used as creative ways to justify that happening.  This is identical to free form play, but with a lot more painful fumbling about added in because apparently thats what you are supposed to do in RPGS (this is sarcasm, I have played many RPGs where the designer had figured out that this is not true).  

I disagree pretty strongly with the idea that story focused gamers will like this game and mechanic focused gamers will be dissatisfied.  First of all, while even have all the mechanical crunchy bits in the game if you already know that they won't be fun to use?  All you are doing is providing false hope for those mechanics focused gamers, and creating annoying distractions for the players who don't care about the mechanics.  Secondly, story vs mechanics, as it is being used in the current discussion is a false dichotomy.  If I am focused on the story, I want the mechanics to back me up, even if I am not paying attention to them.  What actually happens in these kinds of systems is that story focused gamers have to let the GMs interpret their input before they get to see if their story focus matters in the way they want it to matter.  If its the GMs job to step in and ignore the mechanics when they get in the way of the story, thats just another way of saying that the GM drives the story and the players do not.  So story focused gamers get betrayed by the system.

I still have concerns about the Scene Tracker because there have been cases where there have major foes able to accelerate it in addition to its normal progression.  With that it seems things escalate too quickly at times without the players able to do much about it. Overall, I’ve enjoyed what I’ve seen and I’m looking forward to Paul leading his own session. 

 

As per the Starter Kit, players CAN do something about it… unless the scene specifically prevents it, an Overcome roll can be used to prevent the Scene Tracker from advancing during it’s next turn… that would just require one player to dedicate his action to attempting to stabilize the situation, so a coordinated team has a good chance of keeping a scene from escalating too much due to villain activity.

During the first issue on the live playtest, I expected someone to suggest Rae to do just that when the Lazer Dragon started burrowing into the ground, using her powers to delay it’s progress and give them more time to deal with it.
